name: Cube organizer and modular shelving
tagline: Panels and plastic connectors, or a cam-lock grid. The no-tools kind is deceptively easy to build wrong.
covers: Modular wire or plastic cube shelving
peopleNote: One person. A child can genuinely help with this one.

tools.why: Seating plastic connectors and dowels without hurting your palm.
If yours is the wooden cam-lock style rather than the plastic connector style.

before: Work out which type you have. If it came with plastic X-shaped connectors it is the tool-free kind. If it came with an Allen key and metal discs, follow the cam-lock box pattern instead.
Build it flat on the floor, then stand it up. Building a grid standing up is a losing battle.
Decide now whether it goes against a wall. Tall cube units must be anchored.
safety: Cube units are light and children love climbing them. Anchor anything taller than two cubes high.
Never stack two separate cube units on top of each other unless they are designed to connect.

steps.title: Identify which system you have
steps.say: Plastic X or T-shaped connectors means the tool-free kind. Metal discs and an Allen key means it is really a cam-lock box in a grid shape.
do: Look in the hardware bag
Plastic connectors: carry on with this guide
Cam locks and Allen key: the cam-lock box guide is the one you want
steps.tip: A few units are a hybrid, with plastic connectors and screws for the back. Read the parts list.

steps.title: Lay out the grid flat, dry, before connecting
steps.say: Put the panels on the floor in the shape of the finished grid without connecting anything. You will instantly see how it goes together.
do: Outer panels around the edge
Inner divider panels where the cubes split
Compare against the manual picture
steps.tip: Dry-laying the whole thing first takes two minutes and prevents the classic problem of discovering you are a divider short at the far corner.

steps.title: Start with one corner
steps.say: Push a corner connector onto the edge of one panel, then push the second panel into the other side of the connector. Firm, straight pressure.
do: Connector onto panel one, straight on, not angled
Panel two into the other slot
Press until it bottoms out
steps.watch: Angled pressure cracks plastic connectors. If it resists, you are not square to the slot.

steps.title: Build out one row at a time
steps.say: Work along one row completely before starting the next. Each new panel adds stiffness, so the grid gets easier to handle as you go.
do: Complete the bottom row first
Then add the uprights for the next row
Then the next horizontal row
steps.tip: Work on the floor with the back of the unit facing down. Gravity holds everything in place for you.

steps.title: Seat every connector fully
steps.say: Go back over every joint and tap it home with the mallet or the heel of your hand. Half-seated connectors are why these units feel flimsy.
do: Tap each joint, gently
Look for any gap between panel and connector
The grid should feel rigid, not springy
steps.watch: If you can see daylight at a joint, it is not seated. That one joint will be the one that fails.

steps.title: Square the grid and fit the back if there is one
steps.say: Measure the diagonals of the outer rectangle and push until they match. Then fit any back panel, which locks that shape in.
do: Diagonals equal
Back panel on, printed side out
Nails or screws at corners first, then around
steps.tip: Many cube units have no back at all. Those rely on being anchored to the wall for rigidity, which makes the next step more important, not less.

steps.title: Stand it up and anchor it
steps.say: Stand it up where it lives, then strap it to the wall. A cube unit full of books is heavy and has almost no base depth to resist tipping.
do: Stand up with help if it is wide
Find a stud or use a proper anchor
Strap at the top, snug
steps.watch: Cube organizers in children's rooms are among the most commonly tipped furniture there is. They are light, grippy, and exactly the right shape to climb.

steps.title: Drop in the bins and load it
steps.say: Assemble any fabric bins by folding their stiffener panels in, then slide them into the cubes. Heavy things at the bottom.
do: Fabric bins: slide the cardboard stiffeners into their fabric sleeves
Bins into the lower cubes for heavy items
Keep the top row light
steps.tip: If a bin is a tight fit, squeeze it slightly as it goes in. They are usually cut a hair generous on purpose.

steps.title: Final push test
steps.say: Push the top of the unit firmly. With the strap on it should barely move. Any flex means a connector somewhere is not seated.
do: Push at the top corner
Listen for clicks or creaks
Re-tap any joint that moves
steps.tip: Check the strap again after a month. Drywall anchors can settle a little under constant tension.

fixes.a: They are sold separately by every manufacturer and in generic multi-packs. Order spares — if one cracked, the unit is probably under some stress, so check the grid is square.

fixes.q: The whole unit racks and leans like a parallelogram
fixes.a: That is normal for a backless cube unit and exactly what the wall strap is for. Square it, then anchor it. Adding a back panel of thin hardboard also works very well.

fixes.q: The panels will not push into the connectors
fixes.a: You are going in at an angle, or there is a burr in the slot. Line it up dead square and press with your palm, not your fingertips. Check the slot for flashing you can trim with a knife.

fixes.q: A cube is slightly too small for my bins
fixes.a: Measure the cube opening and buy bins to match. Cube sizes vary between brands even though they look standard — a common size is around thirteen inches, but not universally.
Only if the manufacturer says so and only when both are anchored to the wall. An unanchored stack is the least stable furniture arrangement in a house.
